analytic.title: Application of an Adaptive Genetic Algorithm for Task Mapping Optimisation on a Wormhole-based Real-time Network-on-Chip 1 st Jessé Barreto de Barros

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The task mapping problem of real-time applications onto a homogeneous multiple processors system-on-a-chip (MPSoC) is an NP-complete problem that can be addressed using search-based meta-heuristic methods. A particular case is the priority preemptive wormhole-based Network-on-a-Chip (NoC) communication architecture that takes into consideration the end-to-end schedulability analysis. In this paper, we present a Adaptive Genetic Algorithm (AGA) with adaptive parameter control strategies that is capable of efficiently achieving schedulable task placements. In our experiments, we perform analytic methods in different scenarios with multiple synthetically generated real-time applications, as well as various platforms with a ranging number of processors to provide a statistical study comparing our algorithm against a standard genetic algorithm approach.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Embedded devices based on homogeneous Multiprocessors System-on-Chip (MPSoC) [1] are capable of tackling real-time critical applications that require massive parallelism to meet their performance demands. An example of an application with such requirements is present in the crescent area of autonomous self-driving vehicles. In this field, applications require fast responses in a real-time setting, due to their critical nature, allied with the necessity to process a large quantity of data obtained from cameras and sensors.

Network-on-a-Chip (NoC) [2] is a well-established intrachip communication architecture paradigm that consists of an interconnected fabric that allows data exchange between MPSoC processor cores. MPSoCs based on NoCs have the following advantages if compared with bus-based ones: (a) flexibility and high level of abstraction; (b) distributed communication control through the use of routers and links; and, (c) scalability due to high bandwidth increasing with the number of processing cores connected.

Real-Time Network-on-a-Chip (RTNoC) is an NoC, including architectural support for Real-Time Systems (RTS) [3]. This support is required since an RTS correctness depends on both their logically correct and time-bounded results.
An RTNoC provides Quality-of-Service (QoS) for the data exchange between tasks of an application in a real-time setting called Real-Time Applications (RTA).

Examples of designs of RTNoCs [4] [5] hold the following features: (a) wormhole switching strategy that decreases the necessary buffer sizes by dividing the messages into smaller transmission unit called flit and sending these flits in a pipeline manner through the network; (b) 2D mesh-grid topology due to its simplicity; (c) a deterministic and predictable algorithm such as an XY-routing algorithm; also, (d) virtual channels [6] that increase the NoC throughput as well as the predictability of message transmissions by allowing the use of message priority preemption.

The Task Mapping Problem (TMP), also known as Task Scheduling, is approached in this paper as an optimisation problem to reduce the number of tasks that do not comply with their timing requirements under the worst-case scenario. The worst-case scenario is the time instant in which all tasks compete between them to gain access to the NoC resources. Hence, if all tasks are schedulable during the worst-case scenario, they are schedulable under other less pessimistic cases.

TMP is an NP-complete problem in which a brute-force approach is computationally unfeasible [7]. For example, a situation with an application with n tasks to be mapped onto an MPSoC with m processing cores, it reflects onto m n possible task mapping solutions. Where each one of these solutions pairs every one of the tasks with a processor core that executes it. For this reason, the lack of an exact method to obtain fully schedulable task mapping solutions justify the use of soft-computing search-based algorithms. Previous related works have demonstrated that Genetic Algorithm (GA) based approaches are capable of achieving fully schedulable task mapping solutions for real-time wormhole switching based NoC based MPSoCs [8] [9] [10].

This paper presents a novel Adaptive Genetic Algorithm (AGA) with adaptive parameter control strategies that adjust its parameters in execution time, being capable of achieving schedulable task placements. In our experiments, we applied both our proposed AGA and the previously used GA to obtain near-optimal task mappings with a reduced number of unschedulable tasks for several scenarios that include the usage of synthetically generated real-time applications mapped onto various platforms with a ranging number of processors. In this direction, we provide a statistical study comparing our algorithm results against those from a standard GA approach.

This paper is organised as follow: Section II explains the system model and the static schedulability test used to tackle TMP as an optimisation problem, Section III briefly describes the standard genetic algorithm (GA) as used in previous works such as [8] [9], and Section IV presents our proposed adaptive genetic algorithm (AGA) as an alternative for GA. Section V introduces the experimental setup used to compare task mappers based on both GA as well as our proposed AGA using a Wilcoxon statistical test to analyze the results. At last, Section VI concludes this paper and points out some of the findings observed in our experiment's results.

div.head: II. TASK MAPPING AS AN OPTIMISATION PROBLEM
div.p: In this paper, we use the End-to-End Response Time (EERT) static schedulability test, as presented in [10], to perform fast evaluations of the quality of different task placements onto the MPSoC. This schedulability test uses a model for both application and NoC-based MPSoC platform to analyze offline the timing behaviour for the RTA tasks and their transmitted messages to check whether, given a task mapping, these tasks responses are bounded by their deadlines.

div.head: A. Platform and Application Models
div.p: The MPSoC platform is modelled as Ψ that is composed of a set of homogeneous processors connected to a Network Interface (NI) Π = {π 1 , π 2 , ..., π n }. Π is connected by a wormhole-based RTNoC formed by a set of routers R = {ρ 1 , ρ 2 , ..., ρ n } and every one of these components are then connected by a set of unidirectional links Λ = {λ π1,ρ1 , λ ρ1,π1 , λ ρ1,ρ2 , ..., λ ρn-1,ρn } in a regular mesh-grid topology. Figure 1 shows a representation of an MPSoC platform using this model.

The RTA is modelled as Ω that is composed of a set of periodic tasks represented as Γ and a set of messages exchanged between these tasks represented as Φ. Each periodic task is modelled as a tuple τ = C, T, D, P, φ represented, respectively, by the task Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), inter-arrival period, relative deadline time,priority-level and φ is a message subdivided in flits sent after the task execution to another task in Γ. Each message, namely a flow of flits, is in turn represented by another tuple φ = τ d , L, Z, K , where τ d is the destination task, L is the basic latency (i.e., the latency for that message when there is no network contention), Z is the message size in flits, and K is the maximum release Jitter for that message that is equal to its source task WCRT defined as R.

The platform and application models have the following assumptions: (a) tasks deadlines are equal to their periods D = T ; (b) tasks transmit a single flow at the end of their execution; (c) each processor π has a processing queue ordered by priority. Therefore, tasks may suffer preemption from tasks with higher-priority mapped to the same processor core. (d) NoC routers have virtual channels with buffers separated by message priority. For this reason, messages are allowed to suffer preemption from messages emitted by tasks with a higher priority that shares the same NoC resources.

div.head: B. Problem Encoding
div.p: A task mapping solution pairs tasks in Γ to processors in Π. It is encoded as a vector of integers M ∈ N |Γ| , where each ith component represents an index(map(τ i )). Figure 2 illustrates the information present in a task mapping solution.

The fitness function unsch, as represented in Eq. 4, receives a task mapping solution, the model for a RTA Ω, and a model for a MPSoC platform Ψ. Then unsch calculates the WCRT, the basic latency, the WCLT for all tasks and messages in Ψ and returns the number of unschedulable tasks.

div.p: III. BRIEF GENETIC ALGORITHM DESCRIPTION Genetic Algorithm (GA) is an evolutionary optimisation heuristic in which search agents are interpreted to be individuals in a population P. Each ith individual holds genetic information called chromosomes and, due to the problem encoding, each chromosome represents a possible mapping solution M i .

These chromosomes are initialised using a uniform random distribution with each chromosome has its components generated randomly in [0, |Π|-1]. After the initialisation step, GA solutions evolve through its iterations, called generations, using three genetic operators: (a) selection; (b) crossover; and (c) mutation.

The selection operator chooses the fittest individuals of the population to transmit their chromosomes to the next generation as parents to their offspring. The selection strategy used is a binary tournament where, to every new offspring, two pairs of different individuals are randomly selected from the population P and the fittest individual of each pair (i.e., the best mapping solution) then become a parent.

GA applies a crossover operator on a pair of parents simulating a reproduction scheme by exchanging chromosomes between them. The crossover operator used is the single-point crossover where, if a pair of parents pass a random check using the crossover rate p c , a random index r ∈ [1, |Γ|] called crossover point is used to separate and swap chromosomes from both parents, to generate two offspring that are new individuals with different mapping solutions. Figure 3 illustrates this crossover operation functionality.

The mutation operator modifies the chromosomes of the offspring individuals obtained by the crossover operator and stimulating the addition of diversity in the solutions. For every jth chromosome, it realises a random test with the mutation rate p m to substitute this chromosome's original value with a new randomly uniform generated mapping index.

After the application of genetic operators, the GA performs an elitist process in which only the fittest individuals so far survives to the next generation, by unifying both parents population: the population from last iteration and the population of offspring P new , resulting in a population P t-1 ∪ P new .

div.head: IV. PROPOSED ADAPTIVE GENETIC ALGORITHM (AGA)
div.p: In this paper, we propose a GA-based algorithm called AGA that has parameter control adaptation strategies capable of changing the crossover and mutation rates used by the genetic operators during the algorithm execution. AGA alters its parameter values using a feedback method that uses a success metric to allow adjustments in the rate in which these parameters change between generations.

The parameters used by the adaptive parameter control strategy, and their suggested values are listed as follows: (a) average crossover rate µ As present in [14], algorithms that contain parameter control strategies to adjust their parameter values have some advantages over their standard fixed-parameter counter-parts. The proposed AGA has the following advantages when compared to the standard fixed parameters GA used in [8] [9] [10]: (a) the adaptive mechanisms eliminate the parameter tuning process in which a time-consuming empirical trial-and-error method is used to find the best parameter for the heuristic before its execution. For example, the work in [9] performs this process to define the best parameters of crossover and mutation rates for GA optimising the task mapping problem tackled here; (b) AGA obtains better results using different parameters during different stages of the search for solutions. For example, a higher mutation rate during the first iteration permits the algorithm to explore for more solutions while at lower mutation rate allows for better exploitation of the known solutions.

Similarly to the standard GA, AGA has a population P . However, each ith individual X i in this population holds their unique crossover and mutation rates p ci and p mi that are used by the genetic operators to generate its chromosome M i , in other words, X i = M i , p mi , p ci .

The initialisation step is analogous to the standard GA, with the addition of the initial setting of parameters for each individual that are set to be equal to the population parameter average p ci = µ Before the application of the genetic operators (described in Section III) the new parameters p mnew and p cnew are generated randomly using a normal distribution for both new offspring individuals, as shown in Eq. 6 and Eq. 7.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULTS
div.p: The proposed experimental setup optimises 9 cases of task mapping problems created from a set of benchmark real-time applications being mapped onto a set of MPSoC platforms with different mesh-grid sizes and numbers of processing cores. For these cases, the following strategies were used : (a) the AGA (present on Section IV) and (b) the GA proposed in [9] and described in Section III with fixed crossover rate of 0.8 and mutation probability of 0.01 .

The used MPSoC platforms have mesh-grid sizes of 3×3, 3×4, 4×4, 4×5, and 5×5, containing respectively 9, 12, 16, 20, and 25 homogeneous processors each. These platforms share the following characteristics: (a) clock of 50 MHz; (b) link width of 32 bits (flits size); (c) link and router latencies to emit a single flit are L λ = 1 cycle and L ρ = 10 cycles, respectively.

The set of applications used is composed of an application used in previous related works (AVA [10]) as well as two randomly generated synthetic real-time applications, with priorities given by the rate-monotonic algorithm. These two synthetic applications (namely, N ormal and U nif orm) have their tasks created using, respectively, a normal and a uniform random distribution for their utilisation factors. Figure 4 shows the distribution of utilisation factors and messages sizes present in all three real-time applications used.

Both GA and AGA were set to evaluate 10000 possible mapping solutions per execution, distributed in their 100 individuals through 100 generations. Since both heuristics are not deterministic, we repeat their execution 32 times, and their best results were then used as samples for statistical analysis.
Table I presents information about the task mapping problems used in our experiment by introducing the platform and application used by each of them.

Figure 5 shows the distribution of results obtained by both AGA and GA during their 32 executions for 9 task mapping problems used. The convergence analysis observes the median convergence history during generations for both AGA and GA during their 32 executions for the optimisation of three task mapping problems from the 9 executed. The selection criterion used is the scenario in which each one of the RTA used is mapped onto an MPSoC platform with the smallest number of processor cores. The following three task mapping problem were selected: (a) TMP1 mapping AVA onto a 3x3 platform with convergence history illustrated in Fig. 6; (b) TMP4 mapping Normal onto a 3x3 platform with convergence history present in Fig. 7; (c) TMP7 mapping application named Uniform onto a 4x4 platform with convergence history represented in Fig. 8;

Figure 6 shows the convergence history for both algorithms during their 32 executions when optimising the task mapping TMP1. Analysing the median behaviour of both algorithms, we observe that, even though they have the same results after 100 generations, their convergence processes are different. During the first half of the total number of generations, we can observe that GA was capable of reaching better solutions than AGA. However, during the second half, AGA could further explore the search-space, achieving better solutions while GA spends most of these iterations stuck in local minimal.

Figure 7 illustrates the median convergence history when optimising TMP4 32 times. In this scenario, the median behaviour for AGA quicker obtains better results than GA. Shortly after 8 generations, GA reaches a minimal local solution with the same evaluation value that AGA is stuck, and both algorithms stay with this best evaluation in the median behaviour. In the 50th generation, AGA was capable of obtaining a better result, and it kept improving its fitness until the last generation obtaining better performance than GA. Meanwhile, after the 50th generation, GA convergence is slower than AGA. It shows that in the median behaviour, AGA was capable of better explore and refine its found solutions than GA when optimising TMP4.

At last, Fig. 8 illustrates the median convergence history when optimising TMP7. In this scenario, similarly to TMP1 optimisation, both AGA and GA reached at the 100th generation task mapping solutions with 7 unschedulable tasks. Therefore, obtaining the same result in the median. However, it is possible to observe that AGA was capable of better explore the search space obtaining a faster convergence than GA. To statistically compare both algorithms, we used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as suggested in [15], available in the non-parametric tests module of software KEEL [16], to determine which algorithm (in our experiments) obtained the best performance.

The test analyses whether the samples obtained from both algorithms executions come from the same population by a hypothesis test (i.e., AGA and GA results are statistically the same). First, it calculates the sum of ranks where AGA outperformed GA R + = 31 and the ones in which the opposite happened R -= 5. Then comparing these rank-sum results with the Wilcoxon distribution table, the p-value calculated is 0.042 exhibiting with a significance α = 0.05. This result means that the null hypothesis was rejected and, therefore, the samples are statistically different, meaning that in our experiments, the AGA outperforms the GA without the necessity of a tuning process due to its adaptability capabilities.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper proposes an adaptive genetic algorithm heuristic that is capable of obtaining competitive results regarding a static parameter genetic algorithm. The algorithms are applied to search possible schedulable task allocation solutions mapping a real-time application onto an MPSoC with a wormholebased NoC.

Moreover, the results obtained from our experiment show that for a set of real-time applications mapped onto MPSoC with different sizes, AGA performs in average significantly better than a GA using the parameters obtained by [9] without the requirement for a parameter tuning process.

As future work, we aim to explore adaptive mechanisms for an even better GA-based algorithm as well as to test their results against a broader range of heuristic algorithms and update our schedulability test to calculate the messages worstcase latency time taking into consideration the routers buffer sizes as present in [17].
